readerTitle: Same poster, two different stores: culture at 500 people
caseNote: 가상 사례 (식료품 체인 매장·물류센터, 레스토랑 그룹) · 적용 레슨, 새 개념 없음
insight: 500명 규모에서 문화는 창업자의 말이 아니라 관리자의 결정, 승진, 규칙, 바쁠 때의 선택을 타고 퍼진다.
misconception: 회사가 커지면 가치를 더 크게, 더 자주 알리면 문화가 유지된다.

sources.text: PPL-06-02 Values in action, PPL-06-04 Culture as you grow 레슨의 개념을 적용
모든 사례와 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 모든 장면(식료품 체인 20개 매장, 레스토랑 12곳, 물류센터 60명, 계산원 재량 $20)은 설명용 가상 설정입니다. 실제 기업이나 통계를 인용하지 않았습니다.
소프트웨어 노트의 '할인 승인 권한' 예시는 일반적인 설명이며 특정 기업 사례가 아닙니다.

cards.title: Same poster, two different stores.
body: At Store 4, a customer's eggs are cracked. The cashier swaps them and says sorry. Ten seconds.
At Store 11, same chain, same problem. The cashier says she needs a manager. The manager is on break. The customer waits, then leaves.
Both break rooms have the same poster: *We make it right.*

image.label: Two grocery checkouts under the same values poster
image.brief: 화면을 반으로 나눈 일러스트. 왼쪽 계산대에서는 직원이 웃으며 달걀을 바로 교환, 오른쪽 계산대에서는 손님이 시계를 보며 기다림. 양쪽 벽에 똑같은 포스터 "We make it right". 실제 마트 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: You run 20 stores and about 500 people.
body: Your grocery chain grew fast. Stores now feel very different from each other, and customers notice.

options.text: Relaunch the values: new posters, a launch video, a values card on every badge
options.feedback: It's visible and quick, but staff believe what managers do, not what posters say. **Values in action** means a value shows up in decisions, especially ones that cost something.

options.text: Let every cashier fix a problem up to $20 without approval, and tell managers to back them
options.feedback: This turns "make it right" into a decision anyone can make. It spreads through a rule and through managers, which is how **culture as you grow** has to travel.

options.text: Spend the next three months visiting every store yourself
options.feedback: It shows you care, and you'll learn a lot. But at 500 people your presence fades the week you leave. Culture has to live in managers and systems, not in your visits.

cards.title: At five people, culture is you. At 500, it's your managers.
body: In a small team, everyone watches the founder. They copy how you treat customers and what you let slide.
At 500, most staff meet you once a year, if ever. They learn what matters from their store manager, the schedule, and who gets promoted.
That's the idea from **Culture as you grow**: culture stops spreading by example and starts spreading through managers and systems. Store 4 and Store 11 got different signals from different managers.

cards.title: Four places people look for the real rules.
body: Staff rarely read the values page. They watch these instead:
list: **Rules and limits:** what you can decide without asking
**Busy moments:** what gets dropped when it's hard
cards.callout: If these four say something different from the poster, people follow these four.
cards.softwareNote: In a software company the same signals show up in who gets promoted and what support or sales staff can approve alone, such as a refund or a discount. Those limits say more about "customer first" than any all-hands slide.

cards.title: Your top manager hits every target.
body: You run 12 restaurants with about 500 staff. One general manager beats his sales targets every month. His kitchen also loses cooks faster than any other, and people who quit mention shouting.
A regional manager job opens. He wants it.

options.text: Promote him. The numbers speak for themselves
options.feedback: You get a proven seller in the job. But 500 people learn that results excuse how you treat people, and promotion is the loudest signal of **values in action**.

options.text: Don't promote him now. Explain why, and coach him on how he runs his kitchen
options.feedback: You may lose some short-term sales or even the manager. In exchange, everyone sees that your values count when they cost something.

options.text: Promote him, on the condition that kitchen turnover improves within six months
options.feedback: It names the problem, which helps. But he'd now shape culture across several restaurants while still learning to fix it in one. **Culture as you grow** spreads through managers, including this one.

cards.title: December, and you're behind.
body: Your chain's distribution center has 60 people and one stated value: *Safety first.* Orders are piling up before the holidays.
A shift lead suggests skipping the 10-minute safety check before each shift until January.

options.feedback: You win back some time. Everyone also learns the value holds only when it's cheap, which is the opposite of **values in action**.

options.text: Keep the check and pay for overtime or an extra shift to cover the volume
options.feedback: It costs money in your busiest month. That cost is exactly what makes people believe the value.

options.text: Let each shift lead decide for their own shift
options.feedback: Local judgment usually helps at this size. But a core value is the one thing that shouldn't vary by shift.

cards.title: Same values, not same everything.
body: A downtown lunch spot and a beach café need different habits. If you write rules for everything, values turn into a checklist and staff stop using judgment, the very thing "make it right" needed.
Name the few things that must be true everywhere. Leave the rest to local managers.
And be patient. One promotion decision won't change a culture. A pattern of decisions over a year will.

image.label: A few fixed pillars with flexible rooms built around them
image.brief: 건물 단면 일러스트. 굵은 기둥 세 개("Core values")는 모든 층에 똑같이 서 있고, 기둥 사이 방들은 층마다 다르게 꾸며짐(마트, 식당, 창고). 실제 브랜드 로고 없음.

cards.title: At 500 people, your decisions are the culture.
body: **Recap:** you used *Values in action* (a value is real when it costs something) and *Culture as you grow* (culture travels through managers, promotions and rules, not the founder).
**Try it today:** pick one company value. Write down the last decision where keeping it cost you something. If you can't find one, that's your answer.
